Which brings me to my next point, your statement that in Capitalism «people who work more [...] make more money».

You raise exceptions to the statement «barring the 1%», but I would argue that the statement is false in more cases than it is true. Here's why.

In a capitalist system, it's not “people who work more make more money”, but rather “the more the workers work, the more the entrepreneur makes money”. This is an important distinction, since in most cases the worker is not the entrepreneur: even in South Korea, which is one of the countries with the highest percentage of self-employed workers, they amount to only about 1/3rd of the total employment. In the USA, they are about 1/10th. Moreover, the trend is decreasing worldwide, concentrating entrepreneurship into fewer and fewer hands.

Note that this isn't because of the 1% or because of taxes and social welfare —this is because capitalism by its own nature has a tendency to concentrate capital, as this improves efficiency. 10k people working for a single company is more efficient than 10k self-employed individuals doing the same kind of work: concentration leads to better return-on-investment for the capital, since it allows you to use the workspace and tools more fully than what a single individual could do. And this efficiency, the maximization of the ROI, is the whole point of capitalism.

This has several consequences. The first and foremost is the disconnection between the workers' productivity and their earnings. While this can be (and sometimes is) compensated with production bonuses or piece rates as an addition or alternative to a fixed salary, it's hardly ever used and even when it's used it's hardly ever comparable to the relationship between productivity and earnings for the self-employed. The end result is a minimization of effort on the employee side: workers end up doing just the bare minimum to not incur penalties, and nothing more. Reminds you of something? The only difference is that here it happens within every company, in the communist regimes you described it happens nationally.

More: while the employer/employee relationship should be no different than any other market exchange (with the worker “selling” his working prowess and the entrepreneur “buying” it), it ends up being more akin to the owner/cattle relationship —especially with the larger companies. The main reason behind this is that the contractual power of the two parties is not equal. The work market is not a free market: there's a large pool of people that need to work to survive, and this makes their “price” very low. Hence the solidification of the banking system and the growth of Venture Capital —middlemen that end up absorbing, with very little work, a large part of the money you should be making from your work.

Concerning your objection about the higher and younger death rate in the first half of the 19th century: yes, it was due to several technical reasons. I object to the rural unemployment remark (in fact, the rural life expectancy was around 10 years higher than the one of city dwellers), but all other technical reasons are definitely on point.

If you want to object that it's unfair to conflate the circumstances with capitalism, and simply an effect of lack of planning or understanding, I would remark that the same holds for the technical reasons for the famines in the communist countries. Moreover, as I said, my argument is that the reason why the context for the high death rate changed was not due to goodwill on the side of the entrepreneurs, but because of regulation and workers unionizing. Better housing and sanitation, cleaner air and water, etc don't come because the factory owner decides he wants to treat his workers better —you get it by and large because of improved city planning and better infrastructure, which is generally controlled by the local government; you get it from regulation about the amounts and nature of the pollutants of the manufacturing process, which is again government intervention; ditto for child labor.

In modern times you get similar situations e.g. with fracking. The companies insist that it's safe and clean, but their hypocrisy shows as soon as their personal lands are the ones that risk being affected (hi, Rex!). Regulation is a double-edged sword: it can be used to prevent overextension of the personal greed of a few at the expense of everybody else, but on the other hand it can also be abused in the opposite direction.

Ultimately, and maybe a bit paradoxically, the reason why we can enjoy the benefits of capitalism to the extent that we enjoy them today is because of socialism, not because it ever went to power, but because by simply existing it helps counterbalance the rougher, more extreme edges of capitalism itself —when it manages to do so.
